title: "Is that so?"
hookLine: the story of Hakuin, falsely blamed for a baby, who says "is that so?" and cares for the child

cards: Angry parents are pounding on a temple door. Their unmarried daughter is pregnant, and when they pressed her to name the father, she named the respected Zen master of the village temple. The whole neighborhood has heard.
The parents shout their accusation in his face. The master listens, and says three words: Is that so? No denial.
No speech. The story is told about Hakuin, a Japanese Zen teacher.

teach.b: It's a story people tell about Hakuin, and nobody can say whether it happened as told. But it has traveled because it shows something clearly.
When the baby is born, the family brings the infant to Hakuin and leaves the child with him: you did this, so you raise it. His reputation is gone. People stop coming to hear him.

teach.h: HE TAKES THE BABY, AND CARES.
teach.b: And he takes the baby. He begs milk from neighbors and whatever else the child needs, and looks after the little one with care. Time passes.
Then the young mother can't bear it anymore and tells her parents the truth: the real father is a young man who works in the fish market.
The parents rush back to the temple, ashamed, apologize over and over, and ask for the child back. Hakuin hands the baby over, and says: Is that so? Look at what the three words are doing.
The first time, they aren't agreement, and they aren't a lie. They're a refusal to fight over his own name while a baby needs looking after. The second time, they aren't triumph.
Praise and blame come and go, and he treats them the same, like weather.
Through all of it, the one thing that doesn't change is the care. The story isn't asking anyone to accept every false charge in silence.
Some readers hear it as a story about ego, how little Hakuin needed to be seen as right. Others hear it about attention: whatever people said, he kept his eyes on the child.

how: Zen teachers and Buddhist writers retell the Is that so? story as a teaching on equanimity, and Buddhist teachers present praise and blame alike as passing conditions, an old theme in the Buddha's teaching.

games.q: the parents come back, ashamed, and beg for the child. you're Hakuin, with your name restored. what do you say?
games.why: he hands the baby back with the same three words he used for the blame.

practice: Bring to mind a small criticism you've heard lately, fair or unfair, not the worst one, and notice what rises in the body: heat, a tight jaw, a speech getting ready.
Let it be there, then silently try Hakuin's words, is that so, and breathe in the space they open before any reply. You can still answer later, and correct the record if you need to.

wordCard.voice: Hakuin. The Zen teacher the story gives three words, is that so, for blame and praise alike, while he keeps caring for the child. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: blame and praise, like weather. The care stays the same. Same time tomorrow.
